```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# The corpus is bundled with the suggested sbert package. Without it the
# vignette shows code and prose only.
has_sbert <- requireNamespace("sbert", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      warning = FALSE, eval = has_sbert,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%")
library(hypergraphs)
```

A corpus can be represented as a hypergraph with documents as nodes and
words as hyperedges, and a spectral partition of that hypergraph divides the
documents into topics. The corpus here is the `covid` data of the sbert
package, a Scopus export of `r format(nrow(sbert::covid), big.mark = ",")`
records on COVID-19 and education published between 2020 and 2024. Each
record has an abstract and a publication year.

## Text cleaning

A bibliographic export carries text in its abstracts that is not part of
the abstract. `clean_text()` decodes HTML entities, strips tags, normalizes
typographic characters, and removes bracketed citation numbers, list
markers, URLs, DOIs, trailing copyright notices and bare numbers. It takes
a character vector or a data frame with a text column and returns an
object of the same length or the same rows. A text whose share of
alphabetic characters falls below `min_content` is replaced by the empty
string. The `remove` argument takes additional patterns; here it names the
placeholder that Scopus inserts for a missing abstract.

```{r clean}
abstracts <- clean_text(sbert::covid, column = "Abstract",
                        remove = "no abstract available", min_content = 0.5)
abstracts <- unique(abstracts)
```

```{r clean-values, include = FALSE}
n_placeholder <- sum(grepl("no abstract available", sbert::covid$Abstract,
                           ignore.case = TRUE))
n_unique <- nrow(abstracts)
n_empty <- sum(!nzchar(abstracts$Abstract))
```

The result is a data frame with the same columns as the input. The
`r n_placeholder` placeholder abstracts are now empty, and `unique()` has
collapsed the records that appear more than once, which leaves
`r format(n_unique, big.mark = ",")` records, `r n_empty` of them with an
empty abstract. Empty abstracts are retained at this stage so that the year
column stays aligned with the text.

## Hypergraph construction

`text_hypergraph()` builds a weighted hypergraph from a corpus. With the
default `construction = "bag"` and `nodes = "doc"`, each document is a
node and each word is a hyperedge that contains every document using the
word. With the default `weight = "n"`, the incidence cell of a document and
a word is the count of the word in the document. Tokens are lower-cased
alphabetic strings, so numbers do not enter the vocabulary. Documents
without any remaining token are dropped with a warning.

```{r build}
stops <- c(stop_words_en(), "covid", "pandemic")
hg <- text_hypergraph(abstracts, column = "Abstract", stop_words = stops,
                      min_count = 5L)
hg
```

The stop list contains the English function words of `stop_words_en()`
and the two words that name the subject of every abstract; a word present
in every document does not separate any two documents. Words that occur
fewer than five times in the corpus are excluded by `min_count`. The incidence
matrix has more than a million cells, so the default `sparse = NULL`
stores it as a sparse matrix.

## Number of topics

`hg_cluster()` with `what = "eigenvalues"` returns the leading eigenvalues
of the normalized hypergraph Laplacian (Zhou, Huang and Schölkopf 2006)
and the gap after each. A large gap after the k-th eigenvalue indicates a
partition into k clusters that the structure supports. The first gap
separates the zero eigenvalue of a connected hypergraph from the rest and
says nothing about a partition.

```{r count}
spectrum <- hg_cluster(hg, k = 18, seed = 1, what = "eigenvalues")
spectrum
```

```{r count-values, include = FALSE}
informative <- subset(spectrum, index >= 2 & !is.na(gap))
ranked_gaps <- informative[order(-informative$gap), ]
best_k <- ranked_gaps$index[1:2]
```

The largest gap after the first is the gap after eigenvalue
`r best_k[1]`, `r sprintf("%.4f", ranked_gaps$gap[1])`, followed by the gap
after eigenvalue `r best_k[2]`, `r sprintf("%.4f", ranked_gaps$gap[2])`.
The spectrum therefore supports `r best_k[1]` or `r best_k[2]` clusters.
The partition below uses sixteen clusters, the number of
topics in the structural topic model of this literature reported by Saqr
et al. (2023), so that the two sets of topics can be compared. Sixteen is
a finer partition than the spectrum supports on its own; its justification
is the vocabulary each cluster owns, reported in the last section.

## Partition

`hg_cluster()` embeds the documents in the leading eigenvectors of the
Laplacian and partitions the embedding with k-means. With the default
`type = "zhou"` the Laplacian is built from hyperedge membership alone:
each hyperedge has unit weight and the incidence cells are not read. The
function takes the hypergraph, the number of clusters and a seed, and
returns a data frame with one row per document and its cluster label.

```{r cut}
topics <- hg_cluster(hg, k = 16, seed = 1)
head(topics)
```

## Topic description

`hg_keywords()` ranks the words of each cluster. It takes the hypergraph
and the partition and returns a data frame with one row per cluster and
word, containing the score, the word's share and the number of cluster
documents that contain the word. The print method shows one row per
cluster with its words joined; the returned table itself is the long form.
The default score, `type = "mass"`, is the summed incidence weight that a
cluster's documents place on the word, which under `weight = "n"` is the
word's count within the cluster.

```{r name-default}
hg_keywords(hg, topics)
```

Under the default ranking every cluster lists the same words: learning,
students, education, online and teaching. These are the most frequent
words of the corpus, and they are the most frequent words of every cluster
as well. The `share` column, the fraction of a word's corpus count that
falls in the cluster, separates the clusters. `sort_by = "share"` ranks by
that column, and `min_docs` sets a support floor so that a word owned by a
cluster only because it occurs in a few of its abstracts does not reach
the top. The `type` argument accepts several scores at once and returns
one block of rows per score.

```{r name-owned}
words <- hg_keywords(hg, topics, type = c("frequency", "ctfidf", "centrality"),
                     sort_by = "share", min_docs = 15)
words
```

The three scores are the raw count of the word in the cluster
(`frequency`), the class-based tf-idf of Grootendorst (2022) (`ctfidf`),
and the PageRank of the word in the cluster's own word hypergraph, in
which the cluster's abstracts are the hyperedges (`centrality`; the
default measure). Ten words per cluster are returned by default. Ranked by
share, the three scores return the same owned vocabulary for each cluster
and differ in the order of the words. The sixteen clusters correspond to
distinct literatures: parents and childhood, infection prevention,
systematic reviews, lockdown policy, narrative essays, messaging tools in
Indonesian higher education, industry and recovery, laboratory teaching,
teacher agency, questionnaire validation, Spanish methodological studies,
technology acceptance models, dental and surgical assessment,
disadvantaged households, the spring campus transition, and residency
training.

The keyword table plots as one panel per cluster and score, with one bar
per word.

```{r name-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 40}
plot(words, value = "share")
```

## Topic sizes

`hg_topic_sizes()` counts the documents of each topic and their share of
the clustered documents. With `weights`, a numeric vector named by
document, it also reports the weighted size and share; a citation count
or a repeat count are typical weights. One row per topic.

```{r sizes, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
sizes <- hg_topic_sizes(hg, topics)
sizes
plot(sizes)
```

## Topic coherence and exclusivity

`hg_topic_quality()` scores each topic's top words on two axes, with the
definitions the structural topic model uses (Roberts, Stewart & Tingley
2019), so a hypergraph clustering and a probabilistic topic model can be
compared on the same numbers. The top words are the most probable words of
the topic's documents.

* Coherence is UMass (Mimno et al. 2011): for every pair of top words,
  the log of how often the rarer word's documents also contain the other,
  counted over the whole corpus and summed. It is never positive; closer to
  zero means the words turn up in the same documents.
* Exclusivity is FREX (Bischof & Airoldi 2012): a weighted harmonic
  mean of how frequent each top word is in the topic and how exclusive it is
  to the topic, summed over the top words. Higher means the topic owns its
  words rather than sharing them with the rest of the corpus.

```{r quality, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
quality <- hg_topic_quality(hg, topics, min_docs = 15)
quality
plot(quality)
```

A topic high on both axes has a vocabulary that co-occurs and that no
other topic uses; a topic low on coherence gathers abstracts that share
words but not a subject. `coherence = "npmi"` gives normalized PMI instead
(Bouma 2009; Lau, Newman & Baldwin 2014), and `words =` scores the top
words of a topic model fitted elsewhere with the same measures.

## Soft membership

`hg_membership()` turns the hard partition into a membership of every
document in every topic. Documents are placed in the spectral embedding
that `hg_cluster()` cut, each topic's centre is the mean position of its
documents, and a document's membership in a topic is the fuzzy c-means
weight with fuzziness 2 (Bezdek 1981), the inverse squared distance to
the centre normalized over topics. A document at a centre has membership 1 there;
one halfway between two centres has 0.5 in each. One row per document and
topic.

```{r membership, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
membership <- hg_membership(hg, topics)
head(membership, 16)
plot(membership)
```

```{r membership-values, include = FALSE}
uniform <- 1 / 16
own <- subset(membership, cluster == topic)$membership
first_doc <- subset(membership, node == "doc_1")
first_m <- setNames(first_doc$membership, first_doc$topic)
distance_ratio <- function(a, b) sqrt(first_m[[a]] / first_m[[b]])
ranked_m <- tapply(membership$membership, membership$node,
                   \(m) sort(m, decreasing = TRUE)[1:2])
closeness <- vapply(ranked_m, \(m) 1 - sqrt(m[2] / m[1]), numeric(1))
```

The memberships of a document sum to one over the sixteen topics, so the
uniform value is `r uniform`. The median membership of a document in its
own topic is `r sprintf("%.2f", median(own))`,
`r sprintf("%.1f", median(own) / uniform)` times the uniform value. With
fuzziness 2 a membership is proportional to the inverse squared distance,
so the square root of the ratio of two memberships is the ratio of the
distances. The first document above is
`r sprintf("%.1f", distance_ratio("Cluster 1", "Cluster 2"))` times closer
to topic 1 than to topic 2 and
`r sprintf("%.1f", distance_ratio("Cluster 1", "Cluster 3"))` times closer
than to topic 3. For the median document the nearest centre is
`r round(100 * median(closeness))`% closer than the second nearest, so most
abstracts lie near a boundary between topics, and the hard label records
the side they fell on. The plot shows, per topic,
the distribution of its own documents' membership in it. A compact topic
has its documents well above the uniform value; a diffuse topic sits
close to it.

## Relations between topics

`topic_network()` builds the topic-by-topic co-occurrence network through
shared vocabulary. For each pair of topics it sums, over all words, the
product of the number of documents in each topic that contain the word,
the full-counting aggregation of bibliometric keyword networks. The
`similarity` argument normalizes that sum by the measures of van Eck and
Waltman (2009); `"cosine"` divides it by the geometric mean of the two
topics' totals and lies in [0, 1]. The function returns an edge list with
`source`, `target` and `weight`, the columns Gephi reads, and with
`what = "network"` a `cograph_network`.

```{r relations}
relations <- topic_network(hg, clusters = topics, similarity = "cosine")
head(relations)
```

```{r relations-values, include = FALSE}
all_relations <- topic_network(hg, clusters = topics, similarity = "cosine")
upper_quartile <- unname(quantile(all_relations$weight, 0.75))
```

Every pair of topics shares the corpus vocabulary, so all
`r nrow(all_relations)` cosine weights lie between
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(all_relations$weight))` and
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(all_relations$weight))`. The plot keeps the upper
quartile of the edges, those of weight
`r sprintf("%.2f", upper_quartile)` or more, places the topics with a spring
layout and scales line width by weight.

```{r relations-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 7}
network <- topic_network(hg, clusters = topics, similarity = "cosine",
                         what = "network")
cograph::splot(network, layout = "spring", minimum = upper_quartile,
               edge_width_range = c(0.5, 8))
```

## Summary

The analysis divided `r format(hg$n_nodes, big.mark = ",")` abstracts into
sixteen clusters without embeddings or truncation. The spectrum of the
hypergraph Laplacian supports `r best_k[1]` or `r best_k[2]` clusters; the
finer partition was chosen to match a
published topic model. Ranking words by the share of their corpus count
that falls in a cluster, with a support floor, yields a distinct
vocabulary for each cluster, whereas ranking by frequency yields the corpus
vocabulary for all of them.
